title: PSAT1 integrates ferroptosis resistance and immune evasion to drive hepatocellular carcinoma progression.
abstract: The serine/glycine biosynthesis pathway plays a critical role in tumor progression and has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in cancer. Phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1) is a key enzyme in this pathway and has been implicated in the progression of multiple malignancies. However, the functional significance and underlying mechanisms of PSAT1 in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain largely undefined. In this study, we identify PSAT1 as a critical determinant of ferroptosis resistance in HCC. Elevated PSAT1 expression was positively associated with ferroptosis resistance and poor clinical outcomes in patients with HCC. Both in vitro and in vivo functional assays demonstrated that PSAT1 promotes HCC cell proliferation and suppresses ferroptosis through an HSPA5-mediated adaptive endoplasmic reticulum response. Mechanistically, PSAT1 interacts with and stabilizes BCLAF1, thereby enhancing HSPA5 messenger RNA stability and translation in HCC cells. In addition, PSAT1 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting M2 tumor-associated macrophage polarization and regulatory T cell infiltration. PSAT1 up-regulates NRF2 expression, which directly binds to the CCL5 promoter to enhance CCL5 production and secretion by tumor cells, thereby fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therapeutically, pharmacological inhibition of PSAT1 with aminooxyacetic acid markedly potentiated the antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy. Our study reveals a previously unrecognized role of PSAT1 in coordinating ferroptosis resistance and immune escape in HCC and highlights therapeutic targeting of PSAT1 as a promising strategy for HCC treatment.

title: Elucidating the toxicogenomic mechanisms of DBP exposure on Hepatocellular carcinoma through network toxicology and molecular docking analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUD: This study explored the molecular mechanisms by which dibutyl phthalate (DBP) contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) pathogenesis using integrated network toxicology and bioinformatics.
METHODS: DBP's carcinogenic potential was evaluated with ADMETLAB 3.0 and ProTox3. DBP-related targets were obtained from ChEMBL, SwissTargetPrediction, and PharmMapper; HCC-related targets from GeneCards and OMIM. Overlapping genes were identified by Venn analysis. A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed using STRING and analyzed with Cytoscape to identify hub genes. Functional enrichment analysis (GO/KEGG) was performed with DAVID. Expression validation and survival analysis used TCGA-LIHC and GEO (GSE39791) data. A prognostic nomogram integrating gene expression and clinical variables was developed. Single-cell RNA sequencing (GSE299340) was analyzed with Seurat to examine hub gene expression. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations investigated DBP interactions with core targets.
RESULTS: A total of 242 overlapping genes between DBP-associated and HCC-associated targets were identified. PPI network analysis revealed seven hub genes: KRAS, GRB2, ESR1, HSP90AA1, SRC, EGFR, and TP53. Enrichment analysis indicated significant involvement in cancer-related pathways. Expression analysis in TCGA and GEO datasets confirmed significant dysregulation of GRB2, ESR1, HSP90AA1, and SRC in HCC tissues, which correlated with patient survival outcomes. The prognostic model incorporating these genes showed good predictive accuracy. Single-cell analysis indicated distinct expression patterns of ESR1 (hepatocytes) and HSP90AA1 (immune cells) in HCC. Molecular docking demonstrated stable binding of DBP to ESR1 and HSP90AA1 with favorable binding energies (-6.8 and -6.1 kcal/mol, respectively). Molecular dynamics simulations supported the stability of these complexes, with van der Waals interactions being the primary binding force.
CONCLUSIONS: This integrative analysis suggests that DBP exposure may contribute to HCC pathogenesis by modulating core genes and pathways, although these findings are associative and require experimental confirmation. Hub genes, especially ESR1 and HSP90AA1, are potential biomarkers and targets. Direct DBP-protein interactions provide mechanistic insights into HCC etiology.

title: Lactate Homeostasis Disruption Potentiates TACE-Immunotherapy in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Developing strategies that simultaneously overcome chemoresistance and immune suppression remains a major challenge for improving transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Inspired by clinically used CaCO3 microspheres in TACE, we propose an "extracellular buffering-intracellular metabolic disruption" strategy to precisely regulate lactate homeostasis for targeted therapy. Herein, we engineered multifunctional embolic microspheres (SDCa-MSs) co-loaded with calcium carbonate nanoparticles (CaNPs), syrosingopine (Syr), and doxorubicin (DOX) for TACE application. Within the acidic tumor microenvironment, SDCa-MSs buffer extracellular acidity while disrupting intracellular lactate metabolism, thereby simultaneously remodeling extracellular and intracellular pH homeostasis. This coordinated regulation enhances DOX efficacy, induces calcium dyshomeostasis and immunogenic cell death, and ultimately stimulates robust antitumor immunity. In multiple murine HCC models, SDCa-MSs markedly suppress tumor growth, remodel the tumor immune microenvironment, and synergistically enhance the therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy. By integrating metabolic regulation, chemotherapy, and immune activation into a single embolic platform, this work establishes an acid-base homeostasis-regulating strategy for potentiating TACE and provides a conceptual framework for improving locoregional cancer immunotherapy.

title: Immune-Related Biomarkers and an Exploratory Prognostic Signature in Biliary Tract and Gallbladder Cancer.
abstract: Gallbladder cancer is an aggressive biliary tract malignancy associated with poor prognosis and limited molecularly guided treatment options. Chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation play central roles in gallbladder carcinogenesis; however, reproducible computational workflows for identifying immune-related biomarkers remain limited. This study describes an integrated bioinformatic workflow for identifying immune-related differentially expressed genes (IRDEGs) and developing an exploratory prognostic gene signature. Differential expression analysis was performed using dataset-specific R-based workflows, and differentially expressed genes were intersected with immune-related gene sets obtained from ImmPort, InnateDB, and the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB). Gene Ontology, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, and gene set enrichment analyses were conducted to characterize biological functions and signaling pathways. Protein-protein interaction networks were constructed using STRING and Cytoscape; immune-cell infiltration was estimated using CIBERSORT; and prognostic genes were identified through sequential univariate, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox, and multivariable Cox regression analyses. The analysis identified 824 consensus differentially expressed genes, including 312 IRDEGs. These genes were significantly enriched in inflammatory and immune-regulatory pathways, including IL6/JAK/STAT3, nuclear factor of kappa light chain enhancer (NF-κB), Toll-like receptor, and chemokine signaling pathways. CXCL8, IL1B, MMP9, TLR2, S100A8, and S100A9 were identified as key hub genes. Immune-cell infiltration analysis revealed a markedly altered tumor immune microenvironment. An exploratory five-gene prognostic signature comprising CXCL8, S100A9, IL16, MMP9, and CD36 successfully stratified patients according to overall survival risk. This integrated workflow provides a reproducible framework for identifying immune-related biomarkers and developing exploratory prognostic signatures in gallbladder cancer. However, independent clinical cohorts and experimental validation are required before these findings can be translated into clinical applications.

title: Prediction of therapeutic targets and drug candidates for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by network-based computational framework.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, with limited therapeutic options and an urgent need for novel treatment strategies. This study presented a network-based computational framework for in silico genome-wide therapeutic target identification and drug discovery.
METHODS: A network-based computational framework was developed that integrates transcriptomic data from multiple independent PDAC cohorts to construct gene co-expression networks. Prognostic gene signatures were incorporated to identify feature modules via hypergeometric enrichment analysis. Key regulatory genes within these modules were prioritized using multi-metric centrality analysis. Functional relevance of candidate targets was assessed using single-cell ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, genome-wide clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) dependency datasets, and clinical survival analyses. To enable therapeutic translation, this study implemented a transcriptome-guided drug discovery strategy to systematically match pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)-specific gene expression signatures with compound-induced transcriptional profiles from the Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures (LINCS) database. Candidate compounds were ranked using a cross-cohort consensus scoring approach and subsequently evaluated in vitro using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), Western blotting, and cell viability assays.
RESULTS: Comprehensive analysis of multi-cohort PDAC transcriptomic data identified 14 key genes with high network centrality, including three potential oncogenic drivers: Cytoskeleton associated protein 2 like (CKAP2L), kinesin family member 18A (KIF18A), and minichromosome maintenance 10 replication initiation factor (MCM10), which exhibited tumor-specific overexpression and poor prognostic associations. Single-cell RNA sequencing (ScRNA-seq) revealed their predominant expression in epithelial tumor cells, while CRISPR screening confirmed functional essentiality. The transcriptome-guided drug discovery approach matched these targets with LINCS perturbation profiles, identifying mitoxantrone/OTSSP167 (CKAP2L inhibitors), PF-3758309 (KIF18A inhibitors), and vorinostat (MCM10 inhibitors) as candidate therapeutics. Experimental validation using qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assays collectively demonstrated the dose-dependent therapeutic effects of these compounds, showing significant mRNA suppression, corresponding decreases in protein levels, and potent anti-proliferative activity in PDAC cells.
CONCLUSION: This study establishes a robust, network-based framework for therapeutic target discovery and transcriptome-driven drug prediction in PDAC. It identifies three novel, functionally essential oncogenic drivers and proposes clinically actionable compounds, offering a scalable approach for addressing undruggable targets in cancer therapy.

title: Total secondary saponins from Anemone raddeana suppress pancreatic cancer via Caspase-3/GSDME-mediated pyroptosis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is highly lethal and resistant to current therapies, underscoring the need for novel strategies that target regulated cell death. This study aimed to evaluate the anti-PC efficacy of total secondary saponins (TSS) from Anemone raddeana and elucidate the mechanism by which TSS induces pyroptosis.
METHODS: TSS components were characterized by mass spectrometry. Anti-tumor effects were assessed in vitro using human pancreatic cancer cell lines (PANC-1 and AsPC-1 cells) and in vivo using xenograft mouse model. Integrated multi-omics analyses (network pharmacology, proteomics, metabolomics, bioinformatics) identified core components, targets, and pathways. Key findings were validated by molecular docking, immunohistochemistry, and Western blotting.
RESULTS: Mass spectrometry identified 17 C-3 monosaccharide triterpenoid saponins in TSS. Both in vitro and in vivo models confirmed that TSS can significantly inhibit PC cell proliferation by inducing pyroptosis through the Caspase-3/gasdermin E (GSDME) pathway. Multi-omics highlighted hederacolchiside A1 as a core compound and revealed its regulation of inflammation, proliferation, and oxidative stress through the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathways. Molecular docking and Western blotting analysis confirmed activation of downstream pyroptosis mechanisms.
CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that TSS suppresses PC progression by regulating Caspase-3/GSDME-mediated pyroptosis through modulation of PI3K/Akt and NF-κB signaling pathways, supporting its potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for PC.

title: Oral artificial microbio-vaccine triggers synergistic immunogenic cell death induction and tumor microenvironment remodeling for liver cancer therapy.
abstract: Artificial cellular systems, engineered to mimic biological functions, offer a promising platform for advanced drug delivery and immunotherapy. Translating such systems into effective oral tumor vaccines, however, remains challenging due to the harsh gastrointestinal environment, inefficient immune activation, and the toxicity of potent immunogenic agents. To overcome these barriers, we engineered an oral artificial micro bio-vaccine via a hierarchical assembly strategy. Triptolide (TP), an immunogenic cell death inducer, was co-assembled with glycyrrhizic acid (GA), an immunomodulator, into a nanodetoxifying core to facilitate efficient loading into hollow Saccharomyces cerevisiae microcapsules (YC), forming the final aggregate (TP/GA-NYPs). This rational design leverages the YC for gastric protection and gut mucosa-targeting, while the Chitosan shell ensures robust encapsulation. Crucially, the TP/GA core demonstrates a synergistic interplay, in which TP potently induces immunogenic cell death, while GA concurrently remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by suppressing metastasis-related markers and enhancing immunostimulatory cytokine profiles. This spatiotemporally coupled action within a single oral aggregate elicits robust intestinal mucosal and systemic immunity, effectively suppressing liver cancer progression and metastasis while mitigating the systemic toxicity of TP. This work highlights the therapeutic potential of functional aggregates in orchestrating synergistic anti-tumor immunity and offers a versatile platform for oral immunotherapy.

title: GlycoRNA-related cellular program scoring identifies Siglec- and myeloid-associated tumor microenvironments for glycoRNA validation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Glycosylated RNAs (glycoRNAs) represent a recently recognized connection between RNA biology and cell-surface glycobiology. However, whether glycoRNA-related processes are relevant to human tumors remains unclear, partly because direct glycoRNA measurements are not yet available across large cancer cohorts. We therefore used transcriptomic data to identify tumor settings in which glycoRNA-related programs may be most suitable for further experimental validation.
METHODS: We curated a glycoRNA-focused literature evidence base and manually reviewed the top extracted relations to define gene modules related to RNA identity, N-glycan and sialylation pathways, RNA trafficking, and lectin/Siglec recognition. The glycoRNA-related cellular program score is an expression-based composite score representing coordinated glycoRNA-related cellular programs, including RNA processing, glycan biosynthesis, trafficking, and lectin/Siglec recognition. It is designed to prioritize tumor contexts for experimental glycoRNA validation. The score was applied to 9,186 TCGA tumors from 32 cancer types and analyzed together with clinical variables, leukocyte fraction, immune signatures, Siglec/checkpoint/myeloid-axis scores, and non-overlapping sensitivity models. Glioblastoma single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets were used for additional context-level validation.
RESULTS: Higher glycoRNA-related cellular program scores were observed in several tumor types, including stomach adenocarcinoma, glioblastoma, lung adenocarcinoma, esophageal carcinoma, mesothelioma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, and lung squamous carcinoma. Survival analyses did not show robust FDR-significant associations after adjustment for age, sex, stage, and tumor type, suggesting that the score should not be interpreted as a general prognostic biomarker. In sensitivity analyses that removed immune and Siglec-related genes from the predictor, the score remained associated with Siglec-decoder, myeloid, checkpoint, and integrated niche features after adjustment for leukocyte fraction and cancer-type effects. Within-cancer meta-analysis supported these associations across cancer types, although effect sizes varied. In glioblastoma, higher scores were found in tumor, myeloid, mesenchymal, and niche-associated compartments in single-cell and spatial analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: This study presents an expression-based map of glycoRNA-related cellular program across human cancers. The results suggest that glycoRNA-related transcriptional programs tend to occur in immune- and myeloid-enriched tumor microenvironments, particularly those involving Siglec-associated features. These findings prioritize tumor contexts for biochemical, imaging, spatial, and perturbation-based glycoRNA validation.

title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts shape features of lymphocyte aggregation and collagen deposition in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The progression of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is significantly influenced by the tumor microenvironment, in which cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), collagen fibers (CFs), and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) interact to regulate tumor growth and immune infiltration. Understanding the spatial and functional coordination among these components is essential for prognostic assessment.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 335 patients from two tertiary hospitals. Early-stage HCC tissue samples were analyzed using artificial intelligence-based algorithms to quantify TIL fraction and aggregation, while collagen architecture was characterized using multiphoton microscopy (MPM). Moreover, single-cell RNA sequencing was used for functional profiling of CAFs, and multiplex immunofluorescence was applied for spatial validation. The relationship between TILs and collagen features was associated with clinical outcomes. Prognostic models were developed using Cox regression and validated internally and externally.
RESULTS: MPM demonstrated strong co-localization of CFs and TILs, with lymphocytes spatially aligned following collagen orientation within the tumor core. CAF subtypes exhibited heterogeneous expression of extracellular matrix (ECM)-related and lymphocyte-modulatory genes, with ECM-mediated signaling dominating CAF-T/B cell communication. TIL aggregation and CF orientation independently predicted disease-free and overall survival. The multifactorial Fiber-TIL-Clinical model (FTC model) achieved superior predictive performance (area under the curve = 0.902 for early recurrence) by integrating these features with clinical variables.
CONCLUSIONS: The FTC model integrates CF features and TIL characteristics, demonstrating strong performance in predicting HCC recurrence.

title: Targeting circular RNAs to overcome therapeutic resistance in liver cancer: from mechanisms to clinical prospects.
abstract: Primary liver cancer, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), remains a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Therapeutic resistance substantially limits the efficacy of chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and radiotherapy. For example, only approximately 30% of patients with HCC derive clinical benefit from sorafenib, and acquired resistance commonly develops within six months, underscoring the urgent need to clarify the molecular basis of treatment failure. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed RNA molecules with high structural stability and tissue-specific expression. In liver cancer, circRNAs regulate therapeutic resistance through multiple mechanisms that converge on ferroptosis suppression, apoptosis evasion, DNA damage repair, oncogenic signaling, immune escape, and cancer stemness. Beyond the canonical competing endogenous RNA model, this review highlights emerging regulatory mechanisms involving RNA-binding protein interactions, circRNA-encoded functional micropeptides, and circRNA-mediated phase separation. Exosomal circRNAs also facilitate the intercellular transmission of resistant phenotypes and remodel the tumor immune microenvironment. We systematically summarize circRNA-mediated resistance across different therapeutic modalities and critically evaluate the available evidence according to experimental models, in vivo validation, and patient validation. Although circRNAs show potential as biomarkers for predicting therapeutic response and as targets for overcoming resistance, most candidates remain at the preclinical stage. Their clinical translation is constrained by the lack of standardized detection methods, insufficient multicenter validation, and inefficient and inadequately targeted in vivo delivery systems. Because most direct mechanistic evidence is derived from HCC, selected iCCA-related findings are incorporated where available.

title: Designing a tumor landscape-modifying vaccine with a unique TLR2/6 agonist for refractory pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Failure of cancer vaccines in clinical trials has been linked to poor preclinical translatability, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments (TMEs), suboptimal antigen delivery to antigen-presenting cells, limited human MHC antigenicity, and insufficiently safe immune adjuvants. Therefore, this study aimed to design an integrated cancer vaccine and evaluate its efficacy in a KPC orthotopic pancreatic cancer model containing the G12D mutation. A novel immune adjuvant, C-VAX, was developed from the natural Toll-like receptor 2/6 agonist UNE-C1 and covalently linked to a KRASG12D neoantigen and WNT5a, a tumor-associated antigen upregulated in resistant tumors. This integrated vaccine enhanced CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and reduced α-SMA expression in the TME. The therapeutic effects were further enhanced following anti-PD-1 checkpoint blockade. These findings suggest that vaccines targeting tumor antigens and resistance-associated TME components may promote an immune-responsive TME in refractory cancers.

title: Spatial Proteomics Uncovers Immune Cell Neighborhoods and Tumor-Immune Interfaces in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies with dismal prognosis and limited treatment options. The complex interplay between tumor cells and their microenvironment contributes significantly to treatment resistance, yet technological challenges have hindered comprehensive spatial characterization of immune components in PDAC tissues. Here, we performed high-dimensional spatial proteomics using multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI) to quantify 27 protein markers across tissues from twelve treatment-naïve PDAC patients who subsequently underwent adjuvant chemotherapy. We achieved confident single-cell phenotypic mapping of the PDAC ecosystem through deep-learning based segmentation and expert-validated phenotypic annotation. Our analysis revealed significant enrichment of immunosuppressive myeloid populations in patients who eventually experienced disease relapse. Conversely, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells were depleted in these relapse-prone tumors. Using spatial probabilistic topic modeling, we identified eight distinct cellular neighborhoods with unique compositions and functional states, including the enrichment of an immune suppressive neighborhood in relapsed patients. While immunogenic cell neighborhoods were present in both patient populations, analysis of the tumor-immune neighborhoods demonstrated altered functional marker expression profiles, suggesting distinct immune activation in patients who relapsed versus those who did not. Our findings provide a high-resolution spatial atlas of the PDAC immune landscape and identify prognostic microenvironmental signatures that may inform the development of novel immunotherapeutic strategies for this recalcitrant disease.

title: Bulk RNA sequencing deconvolution of early-onset pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma identifies cancer-associated fibroblast subsets associated with survival and tumor microenvironment composition.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal cancer characterized by a high abundance of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which influence therapy response, tumor biology and tumor aggressiveness. CAFs are a heterogeneous cell type and previous single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) of PDAC tumors identified three main CAF subtypes: myofibroblastic, inflammatory and antigen-presenting CAFs (myCAF, iCAF, apCAF, respectively). However, scRNAseq on large patient cohorts is often not feasible due to costs and technical constraints. Therefore, bulk RNAseq deconvolution can be used to computationally infer cell types within the tumor microenvironment. Here, Statescope deconvolution was used to identify different cell types of the tumor microenvironment within an early-onset PDAC cohort, comprising 74 patients aged under 60. Three CAF states were detected (iCAFs, myCAFs and desmoplastic CAFs), and their correlations with microenvironmental components, mutational signatures and survival were explored. iCAFs were associated with classical-like tumor cells, whereas myCAFs and desmoplastic CAFs were correlated with basal-like tumor cells. Desmoplastic CAFs are associated with inflammatory granulocytes/neutrophils, while negatively associating with monocyte-derived macrophages and immature/transitional B cells. No associations were observed between mutational signatures and the abundance of CAF and epithelial tumor subtypes. Interestingly, a high abundance of CAFs, and specifically increased iCAF abundance, was associated with improved survival. Deconvolution of bulk RNA sequencing data, followed by its integration with clinical and biological parameters, provides insights into the heterogeneity of CAF subpopulations in the tumor microenvironment of early-onset PDAC patients and explores potential associations with clinical outcomes.

title: Hepatic stellate cells drive hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-dependent metabolic rewiring and proliferation in hepatocellular carcinoma cells
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most prevalent primary liver cancer in adults and represents the third most common cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. With limited treatment options, HCC remains a major global health problem. The majority of HCC develops in a cirrhotic liver, where the tumor microenvironment (TME) is enriched in fibroblasts derived from activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs). Cell-cell interactions in TME play an important role in metabolic reprogramming, which is increasingly recognized as a crucial driver in HCC proliferation. The tumor-promoting and metabolic effects of HSCs on HCC cells however remain incompletely characterized. Understanding how HSC-HCC interaction regulates HCC proliferation can lead to identification of novel therapeutic targets. Here, we established a Transwell co-culture model of HSCs and HCC cells to investigate how HSC-HCC interactions regulate HCC metabolism and proliferation. Using isotope tracing metabolomics, we show that co-culture with HSCs increases proliferation of HCC cells by rewiring glucose metabolism to increase glycolysis and de novo synthesis of nucleotides. Transcriptomic and immunofluorescence staining analyses revealed that HSCs upregulate hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling in HCC cells, which contributes to metabolic rewiring and HCC proliferation. We further identified H2O2 as a candidate crosstalk signal that could mediate HSC-dependent activation of HIF signaling in HCC cells. Together, these findings reveal a previously overlooked modulatory role of HSC-HCC interaction in metabolism-driven HCC progression. Targeting these pathways may represent a promising strategy to improve HCC treatment.

title: Multiplex-GCN Predicts Clinically Actionable Tumor Microenvironment Subtypes in Pancreatic Cancer
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal cancers worldwide. It has a five-year survival rate of approximately 13%, largely due to late diagnosis, rapid metastasis, and limited therapeutic options. The tumor microenvironment (TME), including immune and non-immune cells, plays a role in PDAC progression and drug resistance. However, molecular characteristics of PDAC based on TME-based subtypes are not well studied. To address this, we developed a multi-layered Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to identify TME-guided PDAC subtypes. First, we constructed a TME reference atlas using single-cell RNA-seq data comprising immune and non-immune cell types. Second, we applied in silico cytometry to estimate cell-type proportions in bulk tumor RNA-seq samples from the Cancer Genome Atlas PDAC patients. Third, we constructed the GCN model integrating the estimated patient-specific cellular proportions with multi-omics datasets, such as gene expression, DNA methylation, copy number variation, and clinical data. Finally, we predicted PDAC subtypes using an unsupervised clustering method on the GCN-based embedding matrices. Our method identified seven PDAC subtypes, which we further grouped into two ecological tumor families. These subtypes exhibited distinct immune infiltration, stromal activity, and malignant epithelial cell abundance. Differential gene expression analysis revealed subtype-specific molecular programs. Survival analysis demonstrated significant differences in overall survival across ecological families and subtypes, highlighting their prognostic relevance. Thus, our method provides a biologically informed framework for patient stratification, with potential implications for advancing precision oncology approaches.
